hints.title: Investment or financing?
lines: Investment = buy/sell/manage real assets (capital budgeting, CAPEX)
Financing = how the cash is raised: debt vs equity, buybacks, dividends
Real value comes mainly from investment decisions

hints.title: Business forms
lines: Sole proprietor and general partners: unlimited liability
Shareholders and limited partners: limited liability
Corporation = separate legal entity; easy to transfer ownership

hints.title: Agency & governance
lines: Agency costs come from separating ownership and control
Fixes: stock-based pay + board, audit committee, auditors, internal controls
Accept a project only if its return > cost of capital

questions.question: Which statement best describes the difference between finance and accounting?
choices: Finance records past transactions; accounting plans for the future
Finance is forward-looking; accounting is mainly historical
Finance and accounting have the same focus
Accounting decides which projects a firm should invest in
Finance only deals with tax compliance
questions.explanation: Accounting = past (recording and reporting). Finance = future (managing resources, investment, capital structure). Finance relies on accounting information.

questions.question: Which of the following is an INTANGIBLE real asset?
questions.explanation: Real assets are needed to run the business. Tangible: factories, machines, inventory. Intangible: patents, brands, copyrights, goodwill. Bonds and loans are financial assets.

questions.question: A financial asset is best described as:
choices: A machine or building the firm uses in production
A contract that gives a claim on future cash or ownership
Any asset with a physical form that can be seen or touched
A patent or brand the firm has developed internally
Cash the firm has already spent on research
questions.explanation: Financial assets are contracts (bank loans, bonds, shares). Tradeable financial assets are called securities.

questions.question: An investment decision is also called:
questions.explanation: Investment decisions = purchase/sale of real assets = capital budgeting = capital expenditure (CAPEX).

questions.question: Which of the following is a FINANCING decision?
questions.explanation: Issuing bonds raises capital, so it's financing. The others spend money on (real or business) assets, so they're investment decisions; lending to a supplier is classed as investing in the slides' quick test.

questions.question: Which of the following is an INVESTMENT decision?
choices: Taking out a five-year bank loan
Selling an airplane it no longer needs
Cutting the dividend to preserve cash
questions.explanation: Selling a real asset is an investment decision (disposing of assets). VC injections, loans, buybacks and dividend policy are financing decisions.

questions.question: Tesla builds a new Cybertruck plant and sells $2 billion of new shares to pay for it. How are these two decisions classified?
choices: Neither is a corporate finance decision
questions.explanation: Building a plant = buying a real asset (investment). Selling shares = raising equity (financing). This is one of the Table 1.1 examples.

questions.question: Which statement about financing decisions is most correct?
choices: Good financing alone is always enough to make a company succeed
Financing choices create most of a firm's value
It can't make a firm succeed, but bad financing can sink it
Financing choices have no effect on the firm at all
Only financing choices show up on the balance sheet
questions.explanation: Real value comes from investment decisions (what the firm does). Financing can't create success on its own, but poor financing can sink a firm.

questions.question: After the global financial crisis, which task became MORE important for financial managers because lending got tighter and capital scarcer?
choices: Capital management and finding alternative funding
Recording historical transactions in more detail
Preparing tax returns as the main priority
Reducing attention to liquidity and cash flow
Cutting back on risk management activities
questions.explanation: Crises mean scarce capital and tighter lending, so capital management (capital structure, allocating resources, alternative funding) gained importance, along with risk, cash flow and strategic planning.

questions.question: Which business form has a single owner who is personally liable for all of the business's debts?
questions.explanation: A sole proprietorship isn't separate from its owner, so the owner has unlimited personal liability.

questions.question: What is the MOST a shareholder of a corporation can lose?
questions.explanation: Limited liability: shareholders can lose only what they invested. When Lehman Brothers failed in 2008, shareholders didn't have to cover its debts.

questions.question: How is a (general) partnership taxed?
choices: It pays corporate tax, then partners pay tax again on payouts
It isn't taxed itself; partners pay personal tax on their share
It is fully tax-exempt as long as it stays small
Only the managing partner pays tax on all the profits
Tax is due only when the partnership is eventually sold
questions.explanation: A partnership is a pass-through: it isn't taxed itself, and each partner pays personal income tax on their share of the profits.

questions.question: A corporation is a separate legal entity. Which of the following can it NOT do on its own behalf?
choices: Sign contracts in its own name
Sue and be sued in court
questions.explanation: As a 'legal person' a corporation can make contracts, borrow, lend, sue, be sued and issue shares, but it can't vote in elections.

questions.question: Public (widely held) corporations are characterized by:
choices: Shares owned only by the founders and their families
Ownership separated from control through a board
No ability to issue new shares to the public
Managers who must own a majority of the shares
questions.explanation: Public companies issue shares that trade on stock markets. Shareholders own the firm but control it only indirectly, through the board of directors.

questions.question: What is the financial goal of the corporation?
questions.explanation: Decision rule: take only actions expected to increase the share price and maximize shareholder wealth / firm value.

questions.question: The cost of capital is also known as:
questions.explanation: Cost of capital = opportunity cost of capital = hurdle rate = the return on an alternative investment of similar risk = the minimum acceptable return.

questions.question: A project is as risky as the stock market, which offers a 10% expected return. The project's expected return is 5%. What should the firm do?
choices: Accept it, since any positive return adds value
Reject it and return the cash to shareholders
Accept it only if financed with debt
Accept it if the managers like it
questions.explanation: Accept only if the project's return beats the cost of capital (10%). 5% < 10%, so reject and let shareholders invest the cash themselves.

questions.question: According to the Fisher Separation Theorem, the firm should:
choices: Follow each shareholder's personal spending preferences
Maximize firm value whatever shareholders' preferences are
Let managers choose whatever maximizes their own utility
Pay out all earnings so shareholders can decide themselves
Avoid any project that some shareholders might dislike
questions.explanation: Shareholders have different preferences and often lack the knowledge to run the business, so the firm's goal is simply to maximize its value.

questions.question: In the agency relationship, the principal and the agent are, respectively:
questions.explanation: Principal = shareholder/owner. Agent = manager entrusted to act for them.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of 'empire building'?
choices: Paying a higher dividend to keep shareholders happy
Buying firms mainly to grow size, power and the CEO's pay
Buying back shares whenever the stock price looks undervalued
Hiring an external auditor to review the accounts
Rejecting a project because its NPV is negative
questions.explanation: Empire building = growing the firm for size, power and pay rather than shareholder value. It's a classic agency cost.

questions.question: Volkswagen's 2015 emissions scandal is used as a lesson about:
choices: Taking on too much debt before the scandal broke
Short-term bonus pressure and weak board oversight
Paying excessive dividends instead of investing
Poor inventory management across its factories
Losses from currency moves in foreign markets
questions.explanation: VW's software cheated emissions tests to hit sales/bonus targets. Weak board oversight, short-term incentives, a top-down culture and no whistleblower protection: a governance failure costing $30B+.

questions.question: Which governance mechanism exists mainly to ensure the accuracy of financial statements and prevent misreporting (as in Enron)?
questions.explanation: Audit committees ensure financial statements are accurate. Other mechanisms: an independent board, external auditors, internal controls.

questions.question: Which bonus design best aligns managers with long-term shareholder value?
choices: Bonuses tied only to revenue growth each year
Bonuses tied to how large the firm becomes
A fixed salary with no incentive component
Bonuses tied to ROE plus stock ownership
Bonuses paid for every acquisition completed
questions.explanation: Tie pay to financial targets (ROE, EBITDA), not just revenue or size, and give stock ownership so managers benefit when the share price rises.

questions.question: An employee buys shares after learning about an unannounced development that will raise the stock price. This is:
questions.explanation: Trading on material non-public information is insider trading.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a real asset?
questions.explanation: A patent is an intangible real asset. The others are financial assets.

questions.question: Which of the following is a financing decision?
choices: Purchasing new machinery to expand production
Acquiring a competitor to increase market share
Selling an airplane the firm no longer needs
Repurchasing the company's own shares from the stock market
Lending to a supplier to help it develop a new technology
questions.explanation: A share buyback changes the firm's capital structure, so it's financing. The rest are investment decisions.

questions.question: According to the chapter, where does the real value of a firm mainly come from?
choices: The amount of debt it carries

questions.question: In a limited partnership, which partners manage the business and have unlimited personal liability?
Which of the following is NOT an advantage of a corporation?
choices: The ability to raise large amounts of money quickly
The owners are personally liable for the firm's debts
It is a separate legal entity from its owners

questions.question: A corporation whose shares are not publicly traded and are owned by a small group of investors, such as the company's managers and their families, is called:
A manager avoids a risky but high-return project to protect their job, even though shareholders would benefit from it. This is an example of:
Which of the following best helps reduce agency problems by making managers partial owners of the firm?
choices: Bonuses tied only to revenue growth
Reducing the size of the board
